subtopic_detail: sequencing adjunctive corticosteroid against the first antibiotic dose in suspected adult bacterial meningitis awaiting imaging
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department at 3 am. A 54-year-old man has been brought in by his wife with 12 hours of headache, fever and neck stiffness, and she says he has become progressively harder to rouse over the past two hours.

He opens his eyes to voice, is confused in his speech, and localises to pain. He has no rash, no focal limb weakness and no papilloedema on fundoscopy, but given his reduced conscious level the department protocol requires computed tomography of the head before a lumbar puncture, and the radiographer has been called in from home with an expected delay of about 40 minutes. He takes no immunosuppressive medication, has no history of central nervous system disease and has had no recent overseas travel. Blood cultures have been taken and two cannulas are in place.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112, blood pressure 138/82, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96 per cent in air, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Glasgow coma scale 12, neck stiffness present, no rash, no focal neurological deficit, no papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 21.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 248 mg/L (less than 5), lactate 3.1 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2), blood cultures taken
data_table.Logistics: Computed tomography of the head required before lumbar puncture, expected delay approximately 40 minutes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Await the computed tomography and lumbar puncture results before giving any antimicrobial therapy
options.rationale: Every hour of delay in this condition increases mortality, and cerebrospinal fluid cell count, protein, glucose and polymerase chain reaction remain informative for hours after antibiotics have started. The imaging requirement exists to make the tap safe, not to postpone treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give ceftriaxone with intravenous aciclovir now and withhold corticosteroid entirely
options.rationale: Aciclovir is a reasonable addition where encephalitic features such as seizures, personality change or focal deficits are present, and may well be added here, but omitting dexamethasone discards a treatment with a mortality benefit. Ceftriaxone alone also leaves Listeria uncovered in an adult over 50. (Source: eTG: Acute Bacterial Meningitis)

options.text: Give vancomycin with meropenem now and add dexamethasone after the lumbar puncture is performed
options.rationale: This broader regimen is reserved for healthcare associated meningitis, neurosurgical patients or regions with high cephalosporin resistant pneumococcus, and it is unnecessarily broad for community acquired disease in Australia. Deferring the steroid until after the tap repeats the timing error that removes its benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give dexamethasone with the first dose of ceftriaxone and benzylpenicillin now
options.rationale: Antibiotics must not be delayed for imaging or lumbar puncture when meningitis is suspected and the conscious level is falling, and adjunctive dexamethasone reduces mortality and hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis when given before or with the first dose. Benzylpenicillin is added to ceftriaxone in Australian practice to cover Listeria monocytogenes, which is intrinsically cephalosporin resistant. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give ceftriaxone and benzylpenicillin now and add dexamethasone once the culture confirms the organism
options.rationale: Starting antibiotics promptly is right but the steroid loses most of its benefit once the inflammatory cascade triggered by bacterial lysis is underway, which is why the timing relative to the first dose matters more than the organism. Waiting for culture would place it 24 to 48 hours too late. (Source: eTG: Acute Bacterial Meningitis)

explanation.summary: Community acquired bacterial meningitis in Australian adults is most often pneumococcal or meningococcal, with Listeria monocytogenes contributing in those over 50, pregnant women, and the immunosuppressed, which is why empirical therapy pairs a third generation cephalosporin with benzylpenicillin in those groups. The classical triad of fever, neck stiffness and altered mental state is present in fewer than half of cases, but nearly all have at least two of fever, headache, neck stiffness and altered mental state. Imaging before lumbar puncture is indicated for a reduced or fluctuating conscious level, focal neurological signs, new seizures, papilloedema or immunosuppression, and in every one of those situations antibiotics are given before the scan. Adjunctive dexamethasone blunts the inflammatory response to bacterial lysis and reduces mortality and hearing loss in pneumococcal disease, but only if given before or with the first antibiotic dose. Public health notification and clearance antibiotics for close contacts follow for confirmed meningococcal disease.
key_points: Give antibiotics before imaging whenever imaging would delay treatment.
Add benzylpenicillin to ceftriaxone for Listeria cover in adults over 50, pregnancy and immunosuppression.
Dexamethasone must be given before or with the first antibiotic dose to retain its benefit.
Indications for imaging first are reduced conscious level, focal signs, seizures, papilloedema or immunosuppression.
Cerebrospinal fluid polymerase chain reaction remains positive for hours to days after antibiotics begin.
explanation.pearls: Adjunctive dexamethasone is given as 10 mg intravenously every six hours for four days, and it is stopped if cultures identify an organism other than Streptococcus pneumoniae, since the mortality benefit is confined to pneumococcal disease.

subtopic_detail: choosing the imaging modality for suspected inflammatory back pain in a young adult whose plain films are normal
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 26-year-old man referred with four years of lower back pain that his previous doctor treated as a mechanical injury from his job as a scaffolder.

He says the pain is worst when he wakes and that his back is stiff for about an hour before it loosens, that it eases once he starts moving around on site, and that it wakes him in the second half of the night so he gets up and walks around. Rest over the Christmas break made it worse rather than better. He had a painful red eye treated with drops by an optometrist last year and has intermittent loose stools that he puts down to diet. His C reactive protein is 9 mg/L (less than 5) and his erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 22 mm/h (less than 15). Radiographs of the lumbar spine and pelvis taken last month are reported as normal with no sacroiliac erosion or sclerosis.

data_table.Examination: Reduced lumbar flexion with a modified Schober measurement of 3.5 cm, tenderness over both sacroiliac joints, chest expansion 4.5 cm, no peripheral synovitis, no psoriasis or nail changes
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 9 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 22 mm/h (less than 15), full blood count within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Radiographs of lumbar spine and pelvis reported as normal with no sacroiliac erosion or sclerosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Computed tomography of the sacroiliac joints to assess for erosion and joint space narrowing
options.rationale: Computed tomography shows established bone damage better than plain films but is blind to the active inflammation that precedes it, so a normal study would not exclude early disease. It also delivers a substantial gonadal radiation dose to a young man for information that does not change the next step. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Human leucocyte antigen B27 typing to establish or exclude the diagnosis on genetic grounds
options.rationale: This marker is a useful contributor within the classification criteria but cannot make or exclude the diagnosis alone, since it is carried by around 8 per cent of the Australian population and a minority of carriers ever develop disease. It is interpreted alongside imaging rather than in place of it. (Source: ASAS: Classification Criteria for Axial Spondyloarthritis)
source_refs: ASAS: Classification Criteria for Axial Spondyloarthritis

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine to assess for disc protrusion and nerve root compression
options.rationale: Imaging the lumbar spine looks for the mechanical pathology his previous doctor assumed, and degenerative changes found incidentally would reinforce that label, but his pain improves with activity and worsens with rest, which is the reverse of a discogenic pattern. The sacroiliac joints are where this disease begins and are frequently not covered adequately on a lumbar spine protocol. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Radionuclide bone scan of the whole skeleton to identify areas of increased osteoblastic activity
options.rationale: Scintigraphy lacks both the sensitivity and the specificity required at the sacroiliac joints, where degenerative change and normal variation both produce uptake. It has largely been superseded for this indication by cross sectional imaging. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints including short tau inversion recovery sequences
options.rationale: His features meet the accepted definition of inflammatory back pain, namely onset before 45, insidious onset, morning stiffness beyond 30 minutes, improvement with exercise but not with rest, and night pain that improves on rising, and structural change on plain films takes years to appear. Magnetic resonance imaging detects the active bone marrow oedema of sacroiliitis before any radiographic change, which is what allows the non-radiographic form to be diagnosed and treated. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)
source_refs: ASAS: Classification Criteria for Axial Spondyloarthritis

explanation.summary: Axial spondyloarthritis is characteristically diagnosed eight to ten years after symptoms begin, because young adults with back pain are assumed to have mechanical injury and the plain radiographic changes that define the classical ankylosing form take years to develop. The clinical screen is inflammatory back pain, defined by onset before age 45, insidious onset, morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes, improvement with exercise but not rest, and pain in the second half of the night that eases on getting up. Associated features that raise the probability substantially include anterior uveitis, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, enthesitis, dactylitis, a family history, and a good response to non steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Recognising the non-radiographic form matters because treatment is the same, beginning with regular exercise and a non steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, and progressing to a tumour necrosis factor or interleukin 17 inhibitor when disease activity persists. Inflammatory markers are normal in a substantial minority, so a normal C reactive protein never excludes the diagnosis.
key_points: Inflammatory back pain improves with exercise and worsens with rest, the reverse of mechanical pain.
Structural radiographic change lags symptom onset by years, so normal films exclude nothing.
Magnetic resonance imaging with fluid sensitive sequences detects active sacroiliitis before radiographic change.
Human leucocyte antigen B27 supports the diagnosis but neither confirms nor excludes it alone.
Anterior uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease are the extra-articular features to ask about.
explanation.pearls: A dramatic response to a full dose non steroidal anti-inflammatory drug within 48 hours is itself a diagnostic clue in axial spondyloarthritis, and it is written into the classification criteria as a feature rather than merely a treatment.

sources.label: ASAS: Classification Criteria for Axial Spondyloarthritis

subtopic_detail: deciding anticoagulation duration after a first pulmonary embolism with no identifiable provoking factor
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 47-year-old man in clinic three months after a segmental pulmonary embolism. He has completed three months of apixaban and is asking whether he can stop.

His embolism followed no surgery, no immobilisation, no long haul flight, no trauma and no hospital admission, and he had no active malignancy on a thorough review including up to date bowel screening. He has had no bleeding on treatment, is fully active and back at work as an electrician, and his exercise tolerance has returned to normal. His full blood count, renal and liver function are within normal limits. There is no family history of venous thromboembolism. His echocardiogram at diagnosis showed a normal right ventricle and he has no residual breathlessness.

data_table.Examination: Chest clear, no calf swelling or tenderness, no signs of chronic liver disease
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, renal and liver function within normal limits; no bleeding events on treatment
data_table.Event details: First segmental pulmonary embolism with no surgery, immobilisation, travel, trauma or malignancy identified; normal right ventricle on echocardiography

lead_in: What would you recommend about the duration of his anticoagulation?

options.text: Continue extended anticoagulation indefinitely with periodic review of bleeding risk and benefit
options.rationale: A first unprovoked pulmonary embolism carries a recurrence risk of roughly 10 per cent in the first year and 30 per cent at five years after stopping, and extended anticoagulation reduces that by more than 80 per cent at a low bleeding cost in a patient with no risk factors for haemorrhage. Extended means indefinite with periodic reassessment rather than a fixed further course, because the risk does not fall with time. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE Guidelines)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE Guidelines

options.text: Stop anticoagulation now, since three months is a complete course for a first event
options.rationale: Three months is the complete course for an event provoked by a transient major risk factor such as surgery, where the provoking factor has resolved and recurrence risk falls to around 1 per cent per year. The near pair distinction is entirely whether the event was provoked, which determines whether the risk resolves with the trigger. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE Guidelines)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE Guidelines

options.text: Extend anticoagulation to a total of six months and then stop without further review
options.rationale: Trials comparing six or twelve months against three months show that recurrence is deferred rather than prevented, with the rate after cessation the same whenever treatment stops. A fixed longer course therefore buys time without changing the eventual risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Stop anticoagulation and perform a full thrombophilia screen to guide any further treatment
options.rationale: Thrombophilia testing rarely changes management after an unprovoked event, because the decision to continue already rests on the unprovoked nature of the event, and results are unreliable while a patient is anticoagulated or soon after a thrombosis. Testing is reserved for selected cases such as suspected antiphospholipid syndrome. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE Guidelines)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE Guidelines

options.text: Stop anticoagulation and commence aspirin 100 mg daily as long term secondary prevention
options.rationale: Aspirin reduces recurrence by only around a third compared with more than 80 per cent for a direct oral anticoagulant, so it is a substantially weaker option that is reserved for patients who decline or cannot take anticoagulation. Its bleeding risk is also not negligible, which narrows the apparent advantage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Deciding how long to anticoagulate after venous thromboembolism turns on a single classification: whether the event was provoked by a major transient risk factor, provoked by a persistent one, or unprovoked. Events after surgery, major trauma or prolonged immobilisation resolve with their trigger and are treated for three months, while events associated with active cancer or another persistent risk factor continue while that factor persists. Unprovoked events carry a recurrence risk that does not decline with time off treatment, so extended anticoagulation is offered indefinitely, with a reduced dose of apixaban or rivaroxaban after the initial treatment period providing efficacy with less bleeding. The decision is reviewed periodically against bleeding risk, patient preference, and any change in circumstances, and male sex, a raised D-dimer after cessation and residual vein thrombosis all shift the balance towards continuing. Patients who stop should be taught the symptoms of recurrence and advised on prophylaxis during future high risk periods.
key_points: Three months completes treatment for an event provoked by a major transient risk factor.
Unprovoked events carry roughly 30 per cent recurrence at five years and warrant extended treatment.
Extended anticoagulation means indefinite with periodic review, not a fixed longer course.
Reduced dose apixaban or rivaroxaban is used for the extended phase after the initial months.
Thrombophilia testing rarely alters management and is unreliable during anticoagulation.
explanation.pearls: Extended phase dosing drops apixaban from 5 mg to 2.5 mg twice daily and rivaroxaban from 20 mg to 10 mg daily after the first six months, retaining most of the protection against recurrence while roughly halving major bleeding.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE Guidelines

subtopic_detail: choosing between treatment regimens for latent infection in a person about to start a biologic agent
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar in a pre-biologic screening clinic. A 39-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is due to start a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor and has been screened as part of that workup.

She moved to Australia from Vietnam at age 22 and has no history of tuberculosis treatment or known contact. She is entirely asymptomatic with no cough, fever, night sweats or weight loss. Her interferon gamma release assay is positive, and her chest radiograph shows no parenchymal abnormality, no cavitation, no pleural thickening and no calcified nodes. Two sputum samples induced for completeness are smear negative and cultures are pending at six weeks with no growth to date. Her liver function and full blood count are within normal limits, she takes methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folic acid, and she is not pregnant and is using reliable contraception.

data_table.Examination: Chest clear, no lymphadenopathy, weight stable, synovitis in both wrists
data_table.Investigations: Interferon gamma release assay positive, liver function and full blood count within normal limits, two induced sputum samples smear negative with cultures showing no growth at six weeks
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph with no parenchymal abnormality, cavitation, pleural thickening or calcified nodes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management before she starts the biologic?

options.text: Perform a tuberculin skin test to confirm the result before committing her to any treatment
options.rationale: The skin test is less specific than the interferon gamma release assay, particularly after bacille Calmette-Guerin vaccination which is routine in Vietnam, so a discordant result would create confusion rather than clarity. The blood assay was chosen for exactly this population for that reason. (Source: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

options.text: Treat for latent infection with isoniazid and pyridoxine, with monthly clinical and liver review
options.rationale: A positive interferon gamma release assay with a normal chest radiograph and no symptoms indicates latent infection, and treatment is required before a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor because that class markedly increases the risk of reactivation and of disseminated disease. Isoniazid with pyridoxine for six to nine months is a standard Australian regimen, and pyridoxine is co-prescribed to prevent peripheral neuropathy. (Source: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

options.text: Treat with a four drug regimen of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for six months
options.rationale: This is the regimen for active disease, and using it for latent infection exposes her to four drugs with their combined hepatotoxicity, ocular toxicity and hyperuricaemia for no additional benefit. The distinction rests on her normal radiograph, absent symptoms and negative cultures, which together define latent rather than active infection. (Source: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

options.text: Proceed with the biologic now and monitor with a chest radiograph every three months
options.rationale: Radiographic surveillance detects reactivation after it has occurred rather than preventing it, and tumour necrosis factor inhibitors are associated with rapid progression including extrapulmonary and disseminated disease. Screening exists precisely so that latent infection can be treated before immunosuppression begins. (Source: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

options.text: Repeat the interferon gamma release assay in three months and treat only if it remains positive
options.rationale: The assay is not used serially to confirm itself, and a positive result in a person from a high incidence country reflects genuine prior exposure rather than a laboratory artefact. Repeating it would delay the biologic by three months without changing the decision. (Source: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

explanation.summary: Latent tuberculosis infection means viable organisms held in check by an intact immune response, with no symptoms, a normal chest radiograph and negative cultures, and it carries a lifetime reactivation risk of around 5 to 10 per cent that rises sharply with immunosuppression. Tumour necrosis factor inhibitors are among the strongest drivers of reactivation because tumour necrosis factor alpha maintains granuloma integrity, so screening before starting one is mandatory and treatment of any latent infection should precede or at least begin before the biologic. Screening in Australia uses an interferon gamma release assay in preference to the tuberculin skin test in people vaccinated with bacille Calmette-Guerin, since prior vaccination does not cause a false positive blood assay. Active disease must be excluded before treating latent infection, because monotherapy in unrecognised active disease generates resistance. Regimen options include isoniazid for six to nine months, rifampicin for four months, or combined isoniazid and rifapentine weekly for twelve weeks, with the choice influenced by drug interactions, hepatotoxicity risk and the likelihood of completion.
key_points: Latent infection means a positive immunological test with no symptoms, normal imaging and negative cultures.
Exclude active disease before treating latent infection, since monotherapy would select resistance.
Interferon gamma release assays are unaffected by prior bacille Calmette-Guerin vaccination.
Tumour necrosis factor inhibitors markedly increase reactivation risk including extrapulmonary disease.
Co-prescribe pyridoxine with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy.
explanation.pearls: Rifampicin based regimens induce cytochrome P450 3A4 and render the combined oral contraceptive unreliable for the duration of treatment and for four weeks afterwards, which often decides the regimen choice in a woman of reproductive age.

sources.label: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

subtopic_detail: prioritising which of several contributing medicines to withdraw first after recurrent falls in an older adult
stem:
You are the geriatric medicine registrar reviewing an 84-year-old woman referred after three falls in two months, the most recent causing a wrist fracture. She lives alone, uses a stick outdoors, and describes feeling lightheaded when she gets up from the toilet at night.

Her medications are amitriptyline 25 mg at night started eleven years ago for tension headache and never reviewed, temazepam 10 mg most nights for the past six years, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. Her vision was corrected with new glasses last month and she has no cataract. Her sitting blood pressure is 142/78 falling to 108/62 after three minutes standing, with a pulse rising from 74 to 78. Her timed up and go test takes 18 seconds. Her vitamin D is 68 nmol/L (greater than 50), her corrected calcium is within normal limits, and her sodium is 138 mmol/L (135 to 145).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74 sitting rising to 78 standing, blood pressure 142/78 sitting falling to 108/62 after 3 minutes standing, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Timed up and go 18 seconds, dry mouth, no focal neurological deficit, no cerebellar signs, gait cautious with a stick
data_table.Investigations: Vitamin D 68 nmol/L (greater than 50), corrected calcium within normal limits, sodium 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), full blood count within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Amitriptyline 25 mg at night for 11 years, temazepam 10 mg most nights for 6 years, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, paracetamol as required

lead_in: Which medication change would you prioritise first?

options.text: Cease the atorvastatin, since statins cause myopathy that contributes to falls in older adults
options.rationale: Clinically significant statin myopathy is uncommon and she reports no muscle pain or weakness, so there is no evidence it is contributing here. Removing secondary prevention without a demonstrated harm trades a real benefit for a theoretical one. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Add fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily to treat the postural hypotension directly
options.rationale: Adding a drug to counteract the effect of another drug is a prescribing cascade, and fludrocortisone brings supine hypertension, oedema and hypokalaemia in an older patient. Pharmacological treatment of postural hypotension is considered only after the contributing medicines have been removed and non pharmacological measures have failed. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

options.text: Taper and cease the amitriptyline, since it contributes both anticholinergic burden and postural hypotension
options.rationale: Tricyclic antidepressants are high risk in older adults through anticholinergic effects, sedation, and alpha blockade causing postural hypotension, and at eleven years for a headache indication the benefit is unverified while the harm is now measurable in her postural drop and dry mouth. It contributes to more of her falls mechanisms than any other agent on the list, which is what makes it the priority. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

options.text: Taper and cease the temazepam, since benzodiazepines are the strongest single risk factor for falls
options.rationale: Stopping the benzodiazepine is genuinely important and will be the next step, but a six year habit requires a slow taper to avoid withdrawal insomnia and rebound anxiety, and it does not explain her postural drop. Sequencing withdrawals one at a time also makes it possible to attribute any change to the drug that was stopped. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

options.text: Cease the perindopril, since antihypertensives are the usual cause of postural hypotension
options.rationale: Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors do contribute to postural drops and her dose may well need reducing, but stopping an agent with cardiovascular and renal benefit before removing a drug with no verified benefit at all inverts the risk to benefit reasoning. Her sitting pressure of 142/78 also does not suggest she is over-treated overall. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Falls in older adults are multifactorial, and a structured assessment covers gait and balance, vision, footwear, cognition, continence, home hazards, postural blood pressure, vitamin D status and above all medications. Fall risk increasing drugs include benzodiazepines, antipsychotics, antidepressants including tricyclics and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, opioids, anticholinergics, antihypertensives and hypoglycaemic agents, and risk rises with the total number as much as with any individual agent. Deprescribing works best when it is sequenced rather than simultaneous, starting with the drug that has the weakest ongoing indication and the strongest contribution to the presenting problem, so that any deterioration can be attributed and reversed. Anticholinergic burden deserves specific attention because it accumulates silently across drugs prescribed by different clinicians and contributes to cognitive impairment, urinary retention, constipation and falls. Exercise programmes emphasising balance and strength remain the single most effective non pharmacological intervention for preventing further falls.
key_points: Assess postural blood pressure lying and after three minutes standing in every faller.
Prioritise deprescribing the drug with the weakest indication and the strongest contribution to falls.
Withdraw one drug at a time so that effects can be attributed and reversed.
Long term benzodiazepines require a slow taper to avoid withdrawal insomnia and rebound anxiety.
Balance and strength exercise programmes are the most effective non pharmacological intervention.
explanation.pearls: A timed up and go test taking longer than 12 seconds identifies a person at increased risk of falling and takes under a minute to perform, which makes it the most practical single bedside screen in a busy clinic.

subtopic_detail: setting oxygenation and carbon dioxide targets in the first hours after return of spontaneous circulation in a comatose survivor
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the intensive care unit taking over care of a 58-year-old man who had a witnessed out of hospital ventricular fibrillation arrest 90 minutes ago with bystander compression only cardiopulmonary resuscitation and two defibrillations before return of spontaneous circulation.

He remains comatose, does not obey commands, and is intubated and ventilated. His coronary angiogram on arrival showed an occluded right coronary artery that has been stented, and he is now on a low dose noradrenaline infusion. His current ventilator settings deliver an inspired oxygen fraction of 1.0 and a minute volume set by the retrieval team. The arterial blood gas taken five minutes ago shows a partial pressure of oxygen of 186 mmHg, a partial pressure of carbon dioxide of 28 mmHg and a pH of 7.46, with a lactate of 4.2 mmol/L that is falling from 8.1 mmol/L on arrival.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 in sinus rhythm, blood pressure 102/58 on low dose noradrenaline, respiratory rate 18 ventilated, SpO2 100 per cent, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Comatose and not obeying commands, pupils 3 mm and reactive bilaterally, no spontaneous movement
data_table.Investigations: Arterial partial pressure of oxygen 186 mmHg, partial pressure of carbon dioxide 28 mmHg, pH 7.46, lactate 4.2 mmol/L falling from 8.1 mmol/L
data_table.Ventilator: Inspired oxygen fraction 1.0, minute volume as set by the retrieval team

lead_in: What adjustment to his ventilation would you make now?

options.text: Maintain the inspired oxygen at 1.0 and increase minute volume further to reduce the carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Deliberate hyperventilation was once used to control intracranial pressure but is now avoided because the cerebral vasoconstriction it produces reduces perfusion to injured brain. His carbon dioxide of 28 mmHg is already too low rather than too high. (Source: ANZICS: Post Cardiac Arrest Care)

options.text: Reduce the inspired oxygen to target normal saturation and increase minute volume to clear the lactate
options.rationale: The oxygen adjustment is right but hyperventilating to compensate for a metabolic acidosis treats the number rather than the cause, and his lactate is already falling with restored perfusion. Respiratory compensation driven by the ventilator adds the cerebral vasoconstriction without addressing tissue oxygen delivery. (Source: ANZICS: Post Cardiac Arrest Care)

options.text: Reduce the inspired oxygen to target a saturation of 88 to 92 per cent and leave minute volume unchanged
options.rationale: A saturation target of 88 to 92 per cent belongs to patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and applying it here risks hypoxaemia in a brain that has just sustained a global ischaemic insult. The hypocapnia would also be left uncorrected. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.8: Post-Resuscitation Therapy)

options.text: Reduce the inspired oxygen to target normal oxygen saturation and reduce minute volume to normalise carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Both hyperoxaemia and hypocapnia worsen outcome after cardiac arrest, the first by generating reactive oxygen species during reperfusion and the second by causing cerebral vasoconstriction that reduces blood flow to an already injured brain. Once return of spontaneous circulation is achieved the inspired oxygen is titrated down to a saturation of 94 to 98 per cent and ventilation is adjusted to a normal carbon dioxide of roughly 35 to 45 mmHg. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.8: Post-Resuscitation Therapy)

options.text: Maintain the inspired oxygen at 1.0 and maintain the current minute volume until he wakes
options.rationale: Maximal oxygen is appropriate during the arrest itself when oxygen delivery is the limiting factor, and continuing it afterwards is the anti-pattern this question targets. Sustained hyperoxaemia after return of spontaneous circulation is associated with higher mortality in observational and trial data. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.8: Post-Resuscitation Therapy)

explanation.summary: Post cardiac arrest syndrome comprises brain injury, myocardial dysfunction, a systemic ischaemia and reperfusion response resembling sepsis, and the persisting precipitating pathology, and care in the first hours is aimed at limiting secondary brain injury. Oxygen and carbon dioxide are among the few variables under direct minute to minute control, and both extremes are harmful: hyperoxaemia drives oxidative injury during reperfusion while hypoxaemia deepens the insult, and hypocapnia causes cerebral vasoconstriction while hypercapnia raises intracranial pressure. Targeted temperature management is used to avoid fever, with active control of temperature and treatment of any temperature above 37.7 degrees Celsius. Mean arterial pressure is supported to maintain cerebral perfusion, urgent coronary angiography is performed for ST elevation or a strong suspicion of a coronary cause, and seizures are treated but not prophylactically prevented. Neurological prognostication is deliberately deferred to at least 72 hours after return of spontaneous circulation, and longer if sedation confounds the examination, using multiple modalities rather than a single test.
key_points: Titrate inspired oxygen after return of spontaneous circulation to a saturation of 94 to 98 per cent.
Target a normal carbon dioxide of about 35 to 45 mmHg and avoid deliberate hyperventilation.
Actively control temperature and treat fever, which worsens neurological outcome.
Defer neurological prognostication until at least 72 hours after return of spontaneous circulation.
Arrange urgent coronary angiography for ST elevation or a strong clinical suspicion of a coronary cause.
explanation.pearls: Prognostication at 72 hours relies on several independent modalities together, with bilaterally absent pupillary and corneal reflexes, bilaterally absent N20 somatosensory evoked potentials, a malignant electroencephalogram, and a neuron specific enolase that stays high across serial samples all pointing the same way before any withdrawal decision.
